# Proposed title of this feature request
Enhance CAPZ to Readopt Orphaned Azure VMs by Automatically Recreating AzureMachine Manifests
# What is the nature and description of the request?
When a hosted control plane namespace is deleted as part of a backup/restore process, all AzureMachine CRs are deleted along with it. The underlying Azure VMs, however, continue to exist in the resource group. When the hosted control plane is recreated and etcd is restored from backup, CAPZ has no record of those VMs — no AzureMachine objects are recreated — leaving the VMs unmanaged. CAPZ should be enhanced to scan the cluster's Azure resource group, inspect VM labels to identify VMs that belong to the cluster, and automatically recreate the corresponding AzureMachine manifests to bring those VMs back under CAPZ management.
# Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)
The hypershift project is converging on a unified backup/restore approach outlined in [https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/pull/2004/.|https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/pull/2004/.|smart-link]  That restore path requires deleting the Hosted Cluster and recreating it with etcd restored from a backup. The deletion removes the hosted control plane namespace and all AzureMachine CRs within it, but the Azure VMs remain. Without automatic readoption, CAPZ provisions new VMs on recreation, leaving the original VMs running and unmanaged in the resource group. ARO-HCP intends to adopt this restore path, making this readoption capability a hard requirement.
# List any affected packages or components.
[https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api-provider-azure|https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api-provider-azure|smart-link]

h2. Summary

Two-Node OpenShift with Fencing (TNF) currently supports *only Redfish-compatible BMCs* for STONITH fencing via Pacemaker. 

The Fence Agents Remediation (FAR) Operator — shipped as part of Workload Availability for Red Hat OpenShift — supports a much broader list (see [here|https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/workload_availability_for_red_hat_openshift/4.22-0/html/remediation_fencing_and_maintenance/fence-agents-remediation-operator-remediate-nodes?extIdCarryOver=true&sc_cid=7013a000002w14NAAQ#supported-agents-fence-agents-remediation-operator_fence-agents-remediation-operator-remediate-nodes]) . Esp the coverage of network power devices (APC, Eaton, Emerson, EPS) is highly usefully for TNF edge deployments, e.g. where systems might not have a BMC, but an UPS.  TNF should be enhanced to support the same set of fence agents that FAR supports.

h2. Problem Statement

TNF's Redfish-only fencing limitation restricts the addressable deployment footprint:

# *Bare-metal customers with IPMI-only BMCs* — Many existing server fleets (especially older or low-cost hardware) expose IPMI but not Redfish. These customers cannot use TNF today.
# *Network PDU fencing* — Edge/remote sites often rely on APC or Eaton switched PDUs as the fencing mechanism. These are supported by FAR but not TNF.

The result is that customers must deploy a full 3-node control plane (or TNA with an arbiter) even when their hardware supports proven fencing — just not via Redfish.

h2. Current State (TNF, as of OCP 4.20 Tech Preview)

* Pacemaker + Corosync manage etcd HA outside the cluster
* Fencing credentials collected via install-config.yaml — only Redfish address, username, password, and certificate verification
* Vendor-specific Redfish schemes accepted (idrac-redfish+https://, ilo5-redfish+https://)
* Pacemaker invokes the Redfish BMC to power off an unreachable node (STONITH)

h2. Desired State

TNF should accept fencing configuration for any agent in the FAR-supported set. The full list of agents currently supported in the FAR operator is documented [here|https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/workload_availability_for_red_hat_openshift/4.22-0/html/remediation_fencing_and_maintenance/fence-agents-remediation-operator-remediate-nodes?extIdCarryOver=true&sc_cid=7013a000002w14NAAQ#supported-agents-fence-agents-remediation-operator_fence-agents-remediation-operator-remediate-nodes]. The configuration scheme should follow the FAR configuration approach. 



h2. Proposed Changes

# *install-config.yaml schema* — Extend the fencing.credentials section (currently Redfish-specific) to accept a generic agent field and agent-specific parameter maps, similar to the FenceAgentsRemediationTemplate CR spec. Maintain backward compatibility with existing Redfish-only configs.
# *Pacemaker STONITH resource configuration* — The TNF controller job (triggered by the Cluster Etcd Operator) currently configures a Redfish STONITH resource. Generalize this to configure the appropriate stonith:fence_<agent> resource based on the selected agent and its parameters.
# *Credential handling* — Support the agent-specific parameters each fence agent requires (e.g., IPMI username/password, AWS access keys, VMware vCenter credentials, APC SNMP community strings). Secrets should be stored in a Secret resource, consistent with the FAR pattern.
# *Validation* — Add webhook or install-time validation to ensure the specified agent is in the supported set and that all required parameters for that agent are provided.
# *Documentation and recovery procedures* — Extend TNF installation docs and recovery procedures for new agent types. List of supported agents is documented.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

# TNF install-config.yaml accepts any fence agent from the FAR-supported set with its required parameters
# Pacemaker STONITH resources are correctly configured for each supported agent type
# Fencing (power-off of unreachable node) succeeds for selected supported agent in CI/test environments
# Recovery procedures are documented for each agent type
# Backward compatibility: existing Redfish-only configurations continue to work without modification

h2. Out of scope

# Not all supported fence agents need to be validated in CI/test environments. The assumption is that this is already done on RHEL level  and/or FAR level. One or two selected additional agents which are easy to validate in a CI environment are good enough to validate this.

h2. Summary

Two-Node OpenShift with Fencing (TNF) currently supports *only Redfish-compatible BMCs* for STONITH fencing via Pacemaker. The Fence Agents Remediation (FAR) Operator — shipped as part of Workload Availability for Red Hat OpenShift — already supports *22 fence agents* covering bare metal (IPMI, iLO, iDRAC, BladeCenter), virtualization (VMware, KubeVirt, RHEV), cloud (AWS, Azure, GCE, IBM Power VS, IBM VPC), and network power devices (APC, Eaton, Emerson, EPS). TNF should be enhanced to support the same set of fence agents that FAR supports, enabling TNF deployments across the full range of hardware and cloud environments that Red Hat customers operate.

h2. Problem Statement

TNF's Redfish-only fencing limitation significantly restricts the addressable deployment footprint:

# *Bare-metal customers with IPMI-only BMCs* — Many existing server fleets (especially older or low-cost hardware) expose IPMI but not Redfish. These customers cannot use TNF today.
# *Vendor-specific BMCs* — HP iLO2, IBM BladeCenter, Intel Modular, and Cisco UCS environments have dedicated fence agents in FAR but cannot use TNF.
# *Virtualized environments* — Customers running OpenShift on VMware or RHEV (common in brownfield enterprise datacenters) cannot deploy TNF. KubeVirt nested scenarios are also excluded.
# *Cloud deployments* — While TNF is currently bare-metal-only, aligning the fencing agent interface now would reduce future engineering effort when cloud topologies are considered.
# *Network PDU fencing* — Edge/remote sites often rely on APC or Eaton switched PDUs as the fencing mechanism. These are supported by FAR but not TNF.

The result is that customers must deploy a full 3-node control plane (or TNA with an arbiter) even when their hardware supports proven fencing — just not via Redfish.

h2. Current State (TNF, as of OCP 4.20 Tech Preview)

* Pacemaker + Corosync manage etcd HA outside the cluster
* Fencing credentials collected via install-config.yaml — only Redfish address, username, password, and certificate verification
* Vendor-specific Redfish schemes accepted (idrac-redfish+https://, ilo5-redfish+https://)
* Pacemaker invokes the Redfish BMC to power off an unreachable node (STONITH)

h2. Desired State

TNF should accept fencing configuration for any agent in the FAR-supported set. The full list of agents currently shipped in the FAR operator container image (source: [FAR Dockerfile|https://github.com/medik8s/fence-agents-remediation/blob/main/Dockerfile]):

||Category||Fence Agent(s)||
|*IPMI*|fence_ipmilan|
|*Redfish*|fence_redfish (already supported)|
|*HP*|fence_ilo2|
|*IBM*|fence_ibmblade, fence_ibm_powervs, fence_ibm_vpc|
|*Intel*|fence_intelmodular, fence_amt_ws|
|*Cisco*|fence_cisco_ucs|
|*VMware*|fence_vmware_rest, fence_vmware_soap|
|*RHEV/oVirt*|fence_rhevm|
|*KubeVirt*|fence_kubevirt|
|*AWS*|fence_aws|
|*Azure*|fence_azure_arm|
|*GCE*|fence_gce|
|*Network PDU / Power*|fence_apc_snmp, fence_eaton_snmp, fence_emerson, fence_eps, fence_ipdu, fence_ifmib|

h2. Proposed Changes

# *install-config.yaml schema* — Extend the fencing.credentials section (currently Redfish-specific) to accept a generic agent field and agent-specific parameter maps, similar to the FenceAgentsRemediationTemplate CR spec. Maintain backward compatibility with existing Redfish-only configs.
# *Pacemaker STONITH resource configuration* — The TNF controller job (triggered by the Cluster Etcd Operator) currently configures a Redfish STONITH resource. Generalize this to configure the appropriate stonith:fence_<agent> resource based on the selected agent and its parameters.
# *Credential handling* — Support the agent-specific parameters each fence agent requires (e.g., IPMI username/password, AWS access keys, VMware vCenter credentials, APC SNMP community strings). Secrets should be stored in a Secret resource, consistent with the FAR pattern.
# *Validation* — Add webhook or install-time validation to ensure the specified agent is in the supported set and that all required parameters for that agent are provided.
# *Documentation and recovery procedures* — Extend TNF installation docs and recovery procedures for each supported agent type.

h2. Business Justification

* *Broader addressable market* — Removes the #1 deployment blocker for TNF at edge/remote sites where Redfish is not available
* *Ecosystem consistency* — Aligns TNF fencing capabilities with the Workload Availability stack (FAR), reducing customer confusion about which fencing agents work where
* *Edge/telco demand* — Edge deployments frequently use IPMI-managed servers or PDU-based fencing; these are precisely the environments where a two-node footprint is most valuable
* *Reduced support burden* — Customers attempting to work around the Redfish limitation create unsupported configurations

h2. Acceptance Criteria

# TNF install-config.yaml accepts any fence agent from the FAR-supported set with its required parameters
# Pacemaker STONITH resources are correctly configured for each supported agent type
# Fencing (power-off of unreachable node) succeeds for each supported agent in CI/test environments
# Recovery procedures are documented for each agent type
# Backward compatibility: existing Redfish-only configurations continue to work without modification

* [OKD 4.20 — Preparing to install TNF|https://docs.okd.io/4.20/installing/installing_two_node_cluster/installing_tnf/installing-two-node-fencing.html]
* [FAR Operator — GitHub (medik8s)|https://github.com/medik8s/fence-agents-remediation]

h3. *1. Proposed title of this feature request*

RHACS: Expose Administrative Events as Prometheus Metrics for External Alerting

h3. *2. What is the nature and description of the request?*

 

Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (RHACS) generates "Administrative Events" to log the health and status of the RHACS system itself. These events include critical errors suchas "image scan errors," database issues, or sensor communication failures.

Currently, these events are only visible within the RHACS UI and are not exposed as metrics. This RFE requests that RHACS expose these administrative events, particularly those with a {{level}} of {{ERROR}} or {{WARN}}, as Prometheus metrics.

A new metric, for example, {{rox_central_administrative_events_total}}, could be introduced. This metric should use labels to differentiate the events, such as:

* {{type}}: (e.g., {{image_scan_error}}, {{db_error}}, {{sensor_comm_failure}})

* {{level}}: (e.g., {{info}}, {{warn}}, {{error}})

This would allow external Prometheus instances to scrape these metrics and build alerts based on them.

 

An Alternative Solution might be to have some Integration which alerts for administrative events like there is for policy violations.

h3. *3. Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)*

* *Proactive Incident Management:* The customer's primary requirement is to automatically generate investigation tickets when critical system errors occur. They cannot rely on operators manually monitoring the "Administrative Events" UI page.

* *Ensure Platform Health and Reliability:* Failures logged in Administrative Events (like scan errors) represent a silent failure of the security platform. If new images are not being scanned, the organization is exposed to unknown vulnerabilities. Proactive alerting on these failures is critical to maintaining the platform's reliability and security posture.

* *Reduce Mean Time to Detection (MTTD):* Without metrics, a critical error might go unnoticed for hours or days. Automated alerts based on metrics reduce the detection time to minutes, allowing the platform team to investigate and remediate issues before they cause a significant security gap.

 

h3. *4. List any affected packages or components*

 

* *Metrics Endpoint*
* *RHACS Central*

h3. *1. Proposed title of this feature request*

RHACS: Expose node-level firstDetected timestamp in the API for node vulnerability reporting 

h3. *2. What is the nature and description of the request?*

 

Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security currently exposes node vulnerability data with fields such as CVE {{createdAt}} and node scan information like {{node.scan.scanTime}}.

However, RHACS does not provide a real node-level {{firstDetected}} timestamp in the API showing when a vulnerability was first detected on a specific node.

This makes it difficult to calculate vulnerability age correctly at the node level. Using {{createdAt}} as a fallback is not accurate because {{createdAt}} is not node-specific. It can result in misleading cases, especially when node {{scanTime}} is stale or not refreshed as expected.

This RFE requests that RHACS expose a node-level {{firstDetected}} field for node vulnerabilities in the API.

The requested field should indicate when a given CVE was first detected on a specific node.

h3. *3. Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)*

The customer needs to calculate vulnerability age accurately for node vulnerabilities in external reporting and dashboards.

Currently, we have to approximate {{firstDetected}} using available fields, for example CVE {{createdAt}} and external node creation timestamps. This can be misleading because {{createdAt}} is not node-specific.

We also found cases where CVE data appears newer than the node {{scanTime}}, especially when node scanning has stale {{scanTime}} values. Without a real node-level {{firstDetected}}, it is difficult to distinguish between:

* vulnerabilities newly detected on a node
* vulnerabilities created recently in RHACS data
* nodes with stale or problematic scan timestamps

Having a node-level {{firstDetected}} field would allow accurate age calculation, better prioritization, and more reliable reporting in Power BI / external dashboards.

h3. *4. List any affected packages or components*

* RHACS Central and API

h1. Summary

Add RWX Block volume support as an SBR heartbeat backend, so customers can use the *same* *storage* *class* for SBR as for their VM workloads. The existing RWX File backend must remain fully supported.



  *Acceptance* *criteria*



# SBR can be configured with a StorageClass that provisions RWX Block PVCs, and heartbeat writes/reads succeed across all nodes in the remediation set.

# Node remediation (fence + restart) triggers correctly when a node's heartbeat becomes stale on an RWX Block backend, with failover time comparable to the existing RWX File path.

# The existing RWX File backend continues to function without regression.

# Documentation and Helm/Operator configuration are updated to describe both backend options and recommend "use the same storage class as your VMs" for OCP Virt deployments.



  *Scope* *boundaries*

* *In* *scope:* RWX Block heartbeat backend; configuration surface; documentation; CI test coverage for at least one CSI driver supporting RWX Block.

* *Out* *of* *scope:* Layering a shared filesystem (NFS/CephFS) on top of block volumes; certification matrix for all CSI drivers (follow-on work); changes to RWX File behavior.



  *Risks* *&* *open* *questions*

# Shared-block concurrency: multiple nodes writing to the same block device requires a serialization scheme. Mitigation propsal: Spike needed for candidate approach: per-node block allocation with a metadata block (block 0) mapping nodes

Add RWX Block volume support as an SBR heartbeat backend. This lets customers use the same storage class for SBR as for their VM workloads. The existing RWX File backend must remain fully supported.

h3. Context

Storage Based Remediation (SBR) currently uses a heartbeat backend. The request is to support RWX Block volumes for that backend.

This is for OCP Virt deployments. The documentation should recommend using the same storage class as the VMs.

h3. Acceptance criteria

# SBR can be configured with a StorageClass that provisions RWX Block PVCs.
# Heartbeat writes and reads succeed across all nodes in the remediation set.
# Node remediation, including fence and restart, triggers correctly when a node's heartbeat becomes stale on an RWX Block backend.
# Failover time is comparable to the existing RWX File path.
# The existing RWX File backend continues to function without regression.
# Documentation and Helm/Operator configuration are updated to describe both backend options.
# Documentation and Helm/Operator configuration recommend: "use the same storage class as your VMs" for OCP Virt deployments.
# CI test coverage exists for at least one CSI driver supporting RWX Block.

h3. Other information

In the HyperShift architecture for AWS, configuring a cluster with {{endpointAccess}} set to {{Private}} or {{PublicAndPrivate}}, there currently is no configuration option in the {{HostedCluster}} API to disable PrivateLink in favor of pure routing.

Depending on the customer environment however, AWS policies are in place that prohibit any modifications to VPCs. Consequently, VPC endpoints cannot be created/edited, causing the HCP setup to fail, even though pure routing would already exist which makes PrivateLink/VPC endpoints obsolete.

Adding support for a toggle to disable the creation of PrivateLink in favor of pure routing would solve this problem.

# *Proposed title of this feature request*

Allow users to configure kubelet image credential provider settings ({{--image-credential-provider-config}} / {{--image-credential-provider-bin-dir}}) in MicroShift

# *What is the nature and description of the request?*

We are requesting a way to enable the kubelet image credential provider feature in MicroShift.
Kubelet has a built-in feature called "image credential provider" to get registry login credentials dynamically. (see: [https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-credential-provider/|https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/kubelet-credential-provider/|smart-link] ) This feature can only be turned on through kubelet command-line flags: {{--image-credential-provider-config}} and {{--image-credential-provider-bin-dir}}. There are no matching fields in {{KubeletConfiguration}} (the kubelet config file API).
MicroShift runs kubelet inside a single binary, so users have no way to pass command-line flags to kubelet directly. The {{kubelet:}} section in MicroShift's {{config.yaml}} maps to KubeletConfiguration only, so it cannot cover these flags either.

We would like solutions like below:
• Add {{imageCredentialProviderConfigPath}} and {{imageCredentialProviderBinDir}} fields to MicroShift's {{config.yaml}} and apply them when kubelet starts
• Add an option to the {{microshift run}} command to pass kubelet flags (e.g., {{--kubelet-arg}})

# *Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)*

The customer needs to pull private container images from Amazon ECR on edge devices running MicroShift. Amazon ECR uses short-lived token-based authentication. (see: [aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/registry_auth.html|http://aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/registry_auth.html]) The kubelet image credential provider can automatically refresh these tokens, which is the method AWS officially recommends for pulling images from ECR in Kubernetes.

A workaround exists (periodically updating CRI-O's auth file using a systemd timer), but it requires extra setup and is not as seamless as the kubelet credential provider

# *List any affected packages or components.*

MicroShift 4.20

h3. *Goal Summary:*

ACS includes the ability to evaluate Dockerfile directives.

# ADD directive - must use the COPY command instead of the ADD command

In this case, when the customer’s application Dockerfile does not have an “ADD” directive, it should not violate the “ADD Command used instead of COPY” policy, even if the base image uses an “ADD” directive in its container file.
In addition, a policy can validate using a non-root USER directive in the application layer.

items.fromString:
h2. Summary

Today, when a service's backend pods go down, administrators must drill into *Service details > Pods tab* to discover the issue. There is no health visibility at the list level. This RFE proposes surfacing an aggregated endpoint health indicator directly on the *Services* and *Routes* list pages in the OpenShift Console Networking plugin, enabling faster triage and reducing time-to-detection for degraded services.

----

h2. Problem Statement

The current Services and Routes list pages in OpenShift Console show configuration metadata (name, namespace, labels, selectors, IP/port) but provide *zero indication of backend health*. An administrator managing dozens of services in a namespace has no way to tell — at a glance — which services are actually serving traffic and which have degraded or failed backends.

*Current user journey to check service health:*

# Open Services list page
# Click on a specific service
# Navigate to the "Pods" tab
# Scan individual pod statuses to determine overall service health
# Repeat for every service of interest

This is particularly painful during incidents, when rapid triage across multiple services is critical.

----

h2. Proposed Solution

h3. 1. Endpoint Health Column

Add a *"Health"* column to both the Services and Routes list tables that displays an aggregated endpoint readiness indicator:

||Status||Condition||Visual||
|*Healthy*|All endpoints ready, at least 1 endpoint exists|Green check icon + "3/3"|
|*Degraded*|Some but not all endpoints ready|Yellow warning icon + "2/3"|
|*Down*|No endpoints exist, or all endpoints are not ready|Red error icon + "0/3"|
|*Unknown*|Data not yet loaded|Dash|

*For Services:* The health column shows the readiness of the service's own endpoints.

*For Routes:* The health column shows the readiness of the backing service's endpoints.

h3. 2. Opt-in Health Toggle

Because fetching endpoint data adds API server load, the health column should be *gated behind a toggle*:

* A *"Show endpoint health"* switch in the toolbar area of both list pages
* *Off by default* — preserves current performance characteristics
* When toggled on, endpoint data is fetched and the Health column appears
* Toggle state persists within the browser session

----

h2. User Stories

*US1:* As a cluster administrator, I want to see at a glance which services have degraded or failed backends on the Services list page, so I can quickly identify and triage issues without clicking into each service individually.

*US2:* As a cluster administrator, I want to see the backend health of routes on the Routes list page, so I can identify routes that are pointing to unhealthy services.

*US3:* As a cluster administrator, I want the ability to toggle the health indicators on/off, so the feature does not impose additional API server load when I don't need it.

*US4:* As a cluster administrator, when I scale a deployment down to zero replicas, I want the associated service to immediately show a "Down" status on the list page, so I have instant feedback on the impact of my actions.

----

h2. Acceptance Criteria

# A "Show endpoint health" toggle appears on the Services list page toolbar
# When enabled, a "Health" column appears showing aggregated endpoint readiness (icon + ready/total count)
# A "Show endpoint health" toggle appears on the Routes list page toolbar
# When enabled, a "Backend health" column appears showing the backing service's endpoint readiness
# The toggle defaults to *off* (no extra API load when disabled)
# Toggle state persists across page navigation within the browser session
# Scaling a deployment to 0 replicas results in the service showing "Down" (red) status
# Scaling back up transitions to "Healthy" (green) in real-time
# Services with no selector (e.g., ExternalName) show "Unknown" (dash)
# The health column is responsive and hides on small screen breakpoints
# No performance regression on the list pages when the toggle is off

* Toggle state persists in {{sessionStorage}} (survives tab navigation within a session, but resets on browser close)

h2. Technical Approach

h3. Data Source: EndpointSlices (not Pods)

The health indicator should use *EndpointSlices* ({{discovery.k8s.io/v1}}) rather than watching Pods directly:

* *Lightweight:* EndpointSlice payloads contain only addresses and conditions, not full pod specs
* *Direct signal:* The {{conditions.ready}} boolean on each endpoint is exactly what kube-proxy uses to decide whether to route traffic — it directly answers "is this service serving?"
* *Easy grouping:* EndpointSlices carry a {{kubernetes.io/service-name}} label, so grouping by service requires no selector matching
* *Already used:* The networking console plugin already watches EndpointSlices for the pod traffic indicator on the Service details page

h3. Efficient Fetching (Solving the N+1 Problem)

Rather than one EndpointSlice watch per service (which would create N API watches for N services), the implementation should issue *one namespace-wide EndpointSlice watch*. The results are grouped in-memory by the {{kubernetes.io/service-name}} label and aggregated per service using {{useMemo}}.

When the toggle is off, no watch is established ({{useK8sWatchResource(null)}} — a supported SDK pattern).

h3. Routes: No Extra Watch Needed

For the Routes list, no additional Service watch is required. Each Route already carries {{spec.to.name}} (the backing service name), which maps directly to the {{kubernetes.io/service-name}} label on EndpointSlices. This RFE proposes surfacing an aggregated endpoint health indicator directly on the *Services* and *Routes* list pages in the OpenShift Console Networking plugin, enabling faster triage and reducing time-to-detection for degraded services.

----

h2. Problem Statement

The current Services and Routes list pages in OpenShift Console show configuration metadata (name, namespace, labels, selectors, IP/port) but provide *zero indication of backend health*. An administrator managing dozens of services in a namespace has no way to tell — at a glance — which services are actually serving traffic and which have degraded or failed backends.

*Current user journey to check service health:*

# Open Services list page
# Click on a specific service
# Navigate to the "Pods" tab
# Scan individual pod statuses to determine overall service health
# Repeat for every service of interest

This is particularly painful during incidents, when rapid triage across multiple services is critical.

----

h2. Proposed Solution

h3. 1. Endpoint Health Column

Add a *"Health"* column to both the Services and Routes list tables that displays an aggregated endpoint readiness indicator:

||Status||Condition||Visual||
|*Healthy*|All endpoints ready, at least 1 endpoint exists|Green check icon + "3/3"|
|*Degraded*|Some but not all endpoints ready|Yellow warning icon + "2/3"|
|*Down*|No endpoints exist, or all endpoints are not ready|Red error icon + "0/3"|
|*Unknown*|Data not yet loaded|Dash|

*For Services:* The health column shows the readiness of the service's own endpoints.

*For Routes:* The health column shows the readiness of the backing service's endpoints.

h3. 2. Opt-in Health Toggle

Because fetching endpoint data adds API server load, the health column should be *gated behind a toggle*:

* A *"Show endpoint health"* switch in the toolbar area of both list pages
* *Off by default* — preserves current performance characteristics
* When toggled on, endpoint data is fetched and the Health column appears
* Toggle state persists within the browser session

----

h2. User Stories

*US1:* As a cluster administrator, I want to see at a glance which services have degraded or failed backends on the Services list page, so I can quickly identify and triage issues without clicking into each service individually.

*US2:* As a cluster administrator, I want to see the backend health of routes on the Routes list page, so I can identify routes that are pointing to unhealthy services.

*US3:* As a cluster administrator, I want the ability to toggle the health indicators on/off, so the feature does not impose additional API server load when I don't need it.

*US4:* As a cluster administrator, when I scale a deployment down to zero replicas, I want the associated service to immediately show a "Down" status on the list page, so I have instant feedback on the impact of my actions.

----

h2. Acceptance Criteria

# A "Show endpoint health" toggle appears on the Services list page toolbar
# When enabled, a "Health" column appears showing aggregated endpoint readiness (icon + ready/total count)
# A "Show endpoint health" toggle appears on the Routes list page toolbar
# When enabled, a "Backend health" column appears showing the backing service's endpoint readiness
# The toggle defaults to *off* (no extra API load when disabled)
# Toggle state persists across page navigation within the browser session
# Scaling a deployment to 0 replicas results in the service showing "Down" (red) status
# Scaling back up transitions to "Healthy" (green) in real-time
# Services with no selector (e.g., ExternalName) show "Unknown" (dash)
# The health column is responsive and hides on small screen breakpoints
# No performance regression on the list pages when the toggle is off

# Proposed title of this feature request

[RFE] Isolate ResourceQuota controller synchronization failures to prevent cluster-wide pod creation blockage. ResourceQuota controller should isolate synchronization failures to affected resources/namespaces.

# What is the nature and description of the request?

Enhance the ResourceQuota controller (within kube-controller-manager) to be resilient against partial synchronization failures.

Currently, the controller uses an all-or-nothing approach for its resource monitors. If a single tracked resource (such as a CustomResourceDefinition with a broken conversion webhook or a failing APIService) fails to synchronize, the entire monitor remains in an unsynced state. This causes all ResourceQuota objects in the cluster to lose their {{status.used}} field, resulting in "status unknown for quota" errors that block pod creation across all namespaces.

The request is to implement a mechanism that isolates these failures. For example, if a specific CRD fails to sync, only quotas explicitly tracking that resource should be affected, while standard resource quotas (CPU/Memory/Pods) in unrelated namespaces should remain operational.

# Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)

* *Fault Isolation:* A single misconfigured or stale CRD (for example, from a third-party operator like Oracle WebLogic) should not be able to freeze pod deployments for the entire cluster.
* *High Availability:* Core cluster functionality (scaling and deploying applications) must be resilient to local extension failures. In the current design, a failure in one tenant's resource can impact all other tenants (noisy neighbor effect at the control plane level).
* *SLA Protection:* Customers running large-scale production clusters require that a failure in a non-critical API service does not lead to a total outage of the pod admission system.

# List any affected packages or components

* {{kube-controller-manager}} (specifically the ResourceQuota controller)
* {{openshift-kube-controller-manager}}
* Upstream Kubernetes component: {{pkg/controller/resourcequota}}

I expect to the see the “Critical” “KubeletDown“ alerts fire shortly afterwards but they do not. 

1: deploy pod with exceedingly long termination grace period: {{terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 28800}} 

{noformat}apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: node-metric-down-test
  namespace: ns1
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 28800
  replicas: 0
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-metric-down-test
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      deletionGracePeriodSeconds: 1200
      labels:
        app: node-metric-down-test
        deployment: node-metric-down-test
    spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - /bin/sh
        - -c
        - sleep 1d
        image: docker.io/alpine/curl@sha256:df4d40ffe0bb401d0ed820d00cec452145c4399c5dc52f9d14d327116f1b9b9d
        name: node-metric-down-test
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: 10Mi
          requests:
            cpu: 10m
            memory: 10Mi
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log
        terminationMessagePolicy: File
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 28800{noformat}

3: delete by label, allow pods to scale once again and repeat.. you will soon see alerts for {{TargetDown}} for the Kubelet but not alerts for {{Kubeletdown}}


{noformat}oc -n ns1 delete pods -l app=node-metric-down-test{noformat}

# Proposed title of this feature request

Expose --concurrent as a first-class field in ExternalSecretsConfig

# What is the nature and description of the request?

The upstream External Secrets Operator can define the number of concurrent reconciles as a core controller flag --concurrent. [1]
This is not available with the Red Hat External Secrets Operator (current version 1.1.0 based on the upstream external-secrets project, version v0.20.4) [2]

[1] [https://external-secrets.io/v0.20.4/api/controller-options/|https://external-secrets.io/v0.20.4/api/controller-options/|smart-link] 
[2] [https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.20/html/security_and_compliance/external-secrets-operator-for-red-hat-openshift#external-secrets-operator-rn-1-1_external-secrets-operator-release-notes|https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.20/html/security_and_compliance/external-secrets-operator-for-red-hat-openshift#external-secrets-operator-rn-1-1_external-secrets-operator-release-notes]

# Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)

Secret reconciliation in the customer environment is slow since migrating from the upstream ESO with the current hardcoded value of 1.

In terms of number of resources the customer has the following:
Nodes 40+
ExternalSecret	3700+
ClusterExternalSecret	30+
SecretStore	300+
ClusterSecretStore	6
PushSecret	0

Using the Azure Key Vault with 300+ stores

Beyond just exposing --concurrent, we want to flag that the current ExternalSecretsConfig API provides no supported way to set this parameter in a GitOps-managed environment. We run ArgoCD which reconciles all cluster resources from Git, meaning any direct oc patch deployment is reverted within minutes by either ArgoCD or the Operator itself. We also tested overrideEnv via componentConfigs (introduced in 1.1.0) — the env var is injected but the Operator ignores it and continues hardcoding --concurrent=1 in the deployment args.

The RFE should therefore cover exposing --concurrent as a first-class field in ExternalSecretsConfig (e.g. under spec.appConfig or spec.controllerConfig.componentConfigs), so the Operator translates it into the correct CLI argument during reconciliation.

External Secrets Operator

* In multi-tenant OpenShift environments where network traffic is segregated using EgressFirewall (OVN-Kubernetes), the Custom Metrics Autoscaler (CMA) needs to connect to Kafka clusters located in tenant-isolated namespaces.

*1. Proposed title of this feature request*

* In multi-tenant OpenShift environments where network traffic is segregated using EgressFirewall (OVN-Kubernetes), the Custom Metrics Autoscaler (CMA) needs to pull metrics from data streams (like Kafka, PostgreSQL, or MySQL) located within tenant-isolated namespaces or external CSPs. 
* EgressFirewall rules block this cross-tenant Kafka protocol traffic, making the Kafka scaler unusable in that context.
* While the {{sarama}} Go library (leveraged by KEDA's Kafka scaler) already supports a proxy dialer via {{config.Net.Proxy.Enable}} and {{config.Net.Proxy.Dialer}} (a SOCKS5-compatible {{proxy.Dialer}} from {{golang.org/x/net/proxy}}), the {{kafka_scaler.go}} never exposes or configures these fields. Therefore, users don't have an option to route Kafka scaler traffic through a proxy or gateway.

*2. What is the nature and description of the request?*

* Expose {{proxyAddress}} and {{proxyType}} (e.g., {{socks5}}) as optional metadata fields in the Kafka scaler trigger configuration and/or in TriggerAuthentication, to enable CMA to connect to tenant Kafka clusters, or DB like PostgreSQL, through a SOCKS5 proxy deployed in, or with access to, the tenant's network, without requiring direct network reachability from the CMA namespace.

NOTE: while there's a parallel [RFE-7863]([https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-7863|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-7863]) ("Support for proxy configuration in the Custom Metrics Autoscaler"), that one seemingly covers the broader {{proxy-aware: false}} gap across all scalers. This RFE uses the Kafka scaler as the primary implementation target (since the underlying {{sarama}} library already supports it), but the metadata pattern must be implemented *generically* so other DB scalers like PostgreSQL can use it too.

*3. Currently missing capabilities in current architecture*

# Requirement for Per-Tenant/Per-CRD Proxy Context:
## KEDA currently relies on cluster-wide environment variables (`HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`) applied globally to the controller. To support true zero-trust multi-tenancy, proxy settings must be dynamically configurable at the individual Custom Resource level. This ensures Tenant A's metrics traffic is strictly isolated to Tenant A's proxy, completely independent of Tenant B.

# Support for non-HTTP/TCP Layer protocols (SOCKS5):
## Standard KEDA egress proxy handling is built around HTTP traffic. Because KEDA frequently reaches directly into private databases and message streaming platforms utilizing raw TCP loops, the core network-dialing wrapper must support generic layer-4 TCP proxying protocols like SOCKS5.

# Proposed title of this feature request
## Introduce Continuous Integration (CI) testing and validation workflow for a dedicated {{/var/lib/containers}} disk configurations
# What is the nature and description of the request?
## implement formal CI automated testing, verification, and validation workflows within OpenShift for mounting {{/var/lib/containers}} as a dedicated, separate partition/disk.
Currently, OpenShift documentation and huge amount of field implementations have recommended separating either {{/var}} or {{/var/lib/containers}} to manage storage growth. However, engineering notes that this configuration is not actively validated or tested within OpenShift’s core CI pipelines.
To prevent regressions, ensure accurate file system monitoring ({{imagefs}} counter validation via Kubelet), and confidently support advanced storage topologies, OpenShift needs continuous testing infrastructure that validates cluster stability and cAdvisor/Kubelet eviction monitoring when {{/var/lib/containers}} resides on a separate block device.
# Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)
## Customers are running heavy, modern enterprise workloads, such as *IBM Cloud Paks and large AI/ML workloads,* which consume massive amounts of ephemeral storage. Without a validated mechanism to split disk configurations, a surge in ephemeral storage usage can completely exhaust the root ({{/}}) filesystem, leading to cascading node failures and critical cluster instability.
## To protect clusters from these spikes, enterprise architectures naturally mandate a split-disk setup. However, historical and conflicting documentation recommendations (such as isolating the entirety of {{/var}}, which breaks Kubernetes' {{nodefs}} monitoring) have introduced immense risk. Customers require a fully tested, Red Hat-validated architecture so they can confidently allocate dedicated physical disks to {{/var/lib/containers}} without breaking core Kubernetes metrics.
## Engineering currently recommends a single-partition layout simply because split storage layouts lack a validation pipeline. For Red Hat to officially support and document split-disk layouts—which are vital for large-scale enterprise environments—there must be an automated test suite backing up the architectural advice.
# List any affected packages or components.
## *OpenShift CI / Testing Infrastructure:* Integration of new automated testing suites into the release-blocking or periodic CI pipelines.
## *Kubelet / cAdvisor Monitoring:* Specifically targeting the validation of {{imagefs}} counters and proper pod eviction behavior under separate partition constraints.
## *Machine Config:* Validation that storage layout configurations applied via MachineConfigs accurately provision and maintain the split disk state across upgrades.
## *OpenShift Installer / Assisted Installer:* Ensuring that advanced partitioning schemas during installation can be successfully verified post-deploy.
## *Some OpenShift documentation ref.:*  {{OSDOCS-17206}} and {{OCPBUGS-10640}}.

# Proposed title of this feature request

KEP 4742: Node Topology Labels via Downward API

# What is the nature and description of the request?

The request is for Red Hat OpenShift to adopt and support the upstream Kubernetes [KEP 4742|https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/4742-node-topology-downward-api/README.md] (Node Topology Labels via Downward API) as a standard, supported feature.

# Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)

This would allow workload pods to natively access node topology information via the Downward API without requiring custom, out-of-tree admission controllers or manual synchronization efforts.

User has has a requirement to improve High Availability of these stateful services by adding *topology awareness*, so that the service can:

* On the compute domain: distribute the pods (and their in-memory data), in a way that avoid placing multiple replicas of the same data shard/partition/topic into the same Compute Failure Domain (rack, zone...)
* On the storage domain: also take into consideration the zoning of the storage, avoiding placing replicas of same piece of data into same storage zone (where storage topology supported by CSI / storage backend, not always available)

Some storage backends may support passing topology information on the create volume request (allowedTopologies, supportedTopologies), so that a single StorageClass could suffice.

For stateful services (e.g., Kafka, Cassandra) requiring rack/zone awareness, KEP 4742 provides a native mechanism for pods to discover their failure domain.
- see “racks feature” [https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/5.0.8/cassandra/getting-started/configuring.html|https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/5.0.8/cassandra/getting-started/configuring.html]

# List any affected packages or components.

kube-apiserver (specifically PodTopologyLabelsAdmission plugin)

# Proposed title of this feature request

Add support for graceful handling of certified operator content that lack container image signatures

# What is the nature and description of the request?

Gracefully handle when certified operator container images and bundles are not signed by a partner as opposed to a hard fail error when mirroring certified operator container images.

# Why does the customer need this? (List the business requirements here)

Nearly all OpenShift customers that deploy into disconnected or offline environments use oc-mirror to mirror container content. The content comes from Red Hat and from ceritied partners like NetApp. Because Red Hat does not require parterners to sign their container images in the certified operator catalog, this RFE allows oc mirror to “fail” gracefully when image signatures do not exist for certified operator container images rather than a hard fail.

When oc mirror is set to pull image signatures, as is the default with the release of oc-mirror 4.21, a “hard fail” means that oc-mirror will return an error and no tar archive will be created. Customers must disable image signatures with the oc-mirror CLI flag.

The signature flag for oc-mirror is global and will disable signatures for all content in the imageset-config.yaml, including Red Hat Content. This RFE will allow oc-mirror to handle certified operator content that does not include container image signatures.

# List any affected packages or components.

oc-mirror
